issue.title: feat(pubsub): add client attribution header and pre-release polish
issue.body_html:
• Send gl-dart/<dartVersion> gccl/<packageVersion> in the x-goog-api-client gRPC metadata header on all PubSub requests and verify packageVersion matches pubspec.yaml.
  • Condense CHANGELOG.md into a summary of the initial 0.1.0 feature set.
  • Add the license header and issue_tracker URL to pubspec.yaml.
  • Add .pubignore to exclude protos/ and tool/ from the published package archive.
issue.body_text:
Send gl-dart/<dartVersion> gccl/<packageVersion> in the x-goog-api-client gRPC metadata header on all PubSub requests and verify packageVersion matches pubspec.yaml.
Condense CHANGELOG.md into a summary of the initial 0.1.0 feature set.
Add the license header and issue_tracker URL to pubspec.yaml.
Add .pubignore to exclude protos/ and tool/ from the published package archive.
issue.body:
- Send `gl-dart/<dartVersion> gccl/<packageVersion>` in the `x-goog-api-client` gRPC metadata header on all `PubSub` requests and verify `packageVersion` matches `pubspec.yaml`.
- Condense `CHANGELOG.md` into a summary of the initial `0.1.0` feature set.
- Add the license header and `issue_tracker` URL to `pubspec.yaml`.
- Add `.pubignore` to exclude `protos/` and `tool/` from the published package archive.

docs(pubsub): clarify batching semantics and add end-to-end batching tests

Addresses review feedback on #292:

- Document what `BatchingSettings.maxBytes` actually measures. Only the
  items themselves are counted, so unlike the Python client the per-request
  protobuf and gRPC overhead is excluded. Also document that an oversized
  item is sent alone in a batch that exceeds the limit, and note the
  server-side 10,000,000 byte limit that is not enforced here.
- Correct the default's unit comment: 1024 * 1024 is 1 MiB, not 1 MB.
- Explain the `+ 4` in the modify-ack-deadline item size: each ack ID is
  accompanied by its own int32 deadline in a parallel list.
- Add `batching_e2e_test.dart`, covering behaviour that the fake-based unit
  tests cannot: that a batched publish arrives as N distinct messages with N
  distinct server-assigned ids, that publishes spanning several batches all
  arrive, that `Topic.close()` flushes buffered messages, and that a batched
  acknowledgment actually reaches the server. Each test was verified to fail
  when the behaviour it covers is broken.
- Add a TODO referencing #346 for sharing retry logic with
  `google_cloud_storage`, and clarify that `totalTimeout` is the wall-clock
  budget across all attempts rather than a per-attempt cap.

fix(pubsub): do not drain a request stream that was already listened to

Tearing down a streaming pull connection called `stream.drain()` whenever
`StreamController.hasListener` was `false`. That predicate is `false` in two
very different situations: before the first listener subscribes, and after
that listener has canceled. In the second case `drain()` listens to an
already-consumed single-subscription stream and throws a `StateError`
synchronously, so the trailing `catchError` never ran, the error escaped
`cleanupCurrentConnection`, and reconnection stopped working entirely.

Introduce `DisposableStreamController`, which remembers whether its stream
was ever listened to and therefore only discards undelivered events when
doing so is safe. The drain itself is still required: the future returned by
`StreamController.close()` never completes while the stream has no listener.

This was caught by running the emulator-backed end-to-end suite, where
`streaming_pull_test.dart` failed with `Bad state: Stream has already been
listened to` followed by a 30 second timeout.

TAG=agy
CONV=4ecd3490-bbbe-499e-90e5-07ea5e14a460

fix(pubsub): measure batches the way the server measures requests

Batching counted only the items themselves — message payloads plus attribute
key and value bytes, or bare ack ID lengths. Pub/Sub validates the *serialized*
request (`PublishRequest.ByteSizeLong()`), which also includes the topic or
subscription field, the per-item tag and length prefix, and the attribute map
framing. `maxBytes` was therefore measuring something the server does not.

At the 1 MiB default the gap is 0.06% and harmless. It is not harmless once
`maxBytes` is raised: with it set to the documented 10,000,000 the real request
ran between 58 KB and 2 MB over the limit depending on message shape, and an
oversized request fails with a non-retryable INVALID_ARGUMENT that takes the
whole batch with it. Among the official clients we were the only one with
neither exact accounting nor a safety clamp: Python and Java count the framing
exactly, Go approximates and clamps, Node counts naively but clamps to 9 MiB.

More seriously, `AckSettings` shares `BatchingSettings` with publishing, so the
acknowledgment batchers inherited a 1 MiB ceiling against a 512 KB server limit
for `Acknowledge` and `ModifyAckDeadline` — twice what is allowed. Only
`maxMessages: 100` binding first kept this from firing, and because `_onAckBatch`
suppresses errors for fire-and-forget callers the symptom would not have been an
exception but indefinite redelivery of every message in the batch.

Sizes are computed arithmetically rather than by serializing: `itemSize` runs on
every add, and `package:protobuf` offers no cached size, only `writeToBuffer`.
Measured at 0.30 µs versus 0.29 µs for the old count, against 0.98 µs to
serialize.

Also caps settings to the applicable server limit rather than letting them
produce a request that cannot succeed, and corrects the modify-ack-deadline
comment: only `StreamingPullRequest` carries a deadline list parallel to its ack
IDs, so the estimate is conservative on the unary path.

fix(pubsub): address review of the batch size accounting

The CHANGELOG entry claimed resilient streaming pull and stream-routed
acknowledgment batches, neither of which exists on this branch — those bullets
belong to the stacked PR and were dragged in when the commit was moved between
branches. Removed, and the batching entry now states both caps and the fact
that the acknowledgment default dropped from 1 MiB.

`BatchingSettings` promised that a batch is "never knowingly sent over the
limit" a dozen lines before explaining that a single oversized item is sent
alone in a batch that exceeds it. The first is the paragraph a user consults to
decide whether they need to size-check their own messages, so it is now
explicit that they do.

`wire_size_test.dart` asserted against a local copy of the size function
labelled "Mirrors `Topic._publishedMessageSize`", so a change to the real one
would have left all 2,000 random cases green. Moved that function into
`wire_size.dart` as `publishRequestMessageSize` and pointed both the batcher
and the test at it.

The acknowledgment path had no byte-accounting tests at all, though it is the
path where a mistake is invisible: acknowledgments are fire-and-forget, so an
oversized request surfaces as redelivery rather than an exception. Added
`subscription_batching_test.dart`, which measures every recorded request with
`writeToBuffer()`. Its limits are deliberately tight — the fixed per-request
cost has to be a large enough share of `maxBytes` for its omission to change
the batch boundary — and reverting to the old accounting fails three of them.

Also closes a one-byte under-count: a unary `ModifyAckDeadlineRequest` carries
one shared `ackDeadlineSeconds`, whose tag the per-ack-ID estimate only covered
for groups of two or more. Its tag is now charged in the base size.

`varintSize` guarded its precondition with an assert alone, so a release build
would have returned 1 for a negative value that protobuf sign extends to ten
bytes. Currently unreachable — every caller validates first — but it now fails
in the over-estimating direction, which is the safe one for a size limit.

feat(pubsub)!: reject batch settings the server cannot accept

Asking for a `maxBytes` or `maxMessages` above the applicable Pub/Sub limit
used to be capped silently, matching Python, Go and Node. Throwing is better
here: `BatchingSettings` already throws for its other invalid inputs, so
clamping was the odd one out, and a capped value left the settings object
reporting a size that was not the one in use — `topic.publishSettings.batching
.maxBytes` would say 50,000,000 while batches flushed at 10,000,000.

The check cannot live in `BatchingSettings`, because which limit applies
depends on the request, and one instance may legitimately be shared between
`PublishSettings` and `AckSettings`. It is therefore made when the `Topic` or
`Subscription` is constructed, which is the first point at which the answer is
known, and still well before any RPC.

That leaves one case that must not throw. `maxBytes` defaults to 1 MiB, which
suits publishing and exceeds the 512,000 bytes an `Acknowledge` request
allows, so `AckSettings(batching: BatchingSettings(maxMessages: 50))` would
fail over a byte limit the caller never expressed an opinion about.
`BatchingSettings` now records whether `maxBytes` was supplied rather than
defaulted: a value the caller chose is validated, and the default is narrowed.
The field stays a non-nullable `int` with an unchanged default, so this is not
visible in the public API.

timeline.body_html:
Code Review

This pull request enhances the google_cloud_pubsub package by implementing resilient bidirectional streaming pull capabilities, including support for parallel streams, automatic reconnection with exponential backoff, and background batching/routing of acknowledgments and deadline modifications. Feedback on these changes highlights critical issues where asynchronous stream cancellations could throw unhandled StateErrors during ACK or deadline modification writes, potentially causing callers to hang indefinitely. Additionally, a potential duplicate error emission issue was identified in the stream controller's error-handling logic.

I am having trouble creating individual review comments. Click here to see my feedback.

pkgs/google_cloud_pubsub/lib/src/subscription.dart (192-197)

Calling activeStream.add(...) can throw a StateError if the stream has been cancelled asynchronously (e.g., due to a network drop). Since there is no try-catch block around this call, the exception will propagate and prevent resolveBatch() from being called. This will cause any completers associated with the batch to never complete, leading to callers awaiting acknowledge() hanging indefinitely. Wrapping the call in a try-catch block allows it to safely fall back to the unary RPC path.

    final activeStream = _getActiveStream();
    if (activeStream != null) {
      try {
        activeStream.add(grpc.StreamingPullRequest()..ackIds.addAll(ackIds));
        resolveBatch();
        return;
      } catch (e) {
        // Fall back to unary RPC if stream write fails.
      }
    }

pkgs/google_cloud_pubsub/lib/src/subscription.dart (258-269)

Calling activeStream.add(...) can throw a StateError if the stream has been cancelled asynchronously. Without a try-catch block, this exception will propagate and prevent resolveGroup() from being called, causing callers awaiting modifyAckDeadline() to hang indefinitely. Wrapping the call in a try-catch block allows it to safely fall back to the unary RPC path.

        final activeStream = _getActiveStream();
        if (activeStream != null) {
          try {
            activeStream.add(
              grpc.StreamingPullRequest()
                ..modifyDeadlineAckIds.addAll(ackIds)
                ..modifyDeadlineSeconds.addAll(
                  List.filled(ackIds.length, deadline),
                ),
            );
            resolveGroup();
            return;
          } catch (e) {
            // Fall back to unary RPC if stream write fails.
          }
        }

pkgs/google_cloud_pubsub/lib/src/client.dart (540-551)

When cancelOnError is true, controller.addStream forwards any stream error to the controller and then completes its returned future with that error (throwing it). Because this call is inside the main try-catch block, the caught exception will trigger controller.addError a second time. If the user listens to the stream without cancelOnError: true (the default in Dart), they will receive every stream error twice. Wrapping addStream in its own try-catch block to catch and ignore the thrown error prevents this duplicate emission.

          try {
            await controller.addStream(
              responseStream.expand(
                (response) => response.receivedMessages.map(
                  (receivedMessage) => _mapReceivedMessage(
                    receivedMessage,
                    ackHandler: ackHandler,
                    modifyDeadlineHandler: modifyDeadlineHandler,
                  ),
                ),
              ),
              cancelOnError: true,
            );
          } catch (_) {
            // The error has already been forwarded to the controller by addStream.
          }

commit.message:
feat(pubsub): add message and acknowledgment batching with retry infrastructure

- Add BatchingSettings, PublishSettings, and AckSettings.
- Add background message batching for Topic.publish.
- Add background acknowledgment and deadline modification batching for Subscription.acknowledge and Subscription.modifyAckDeadline.
- Add close() lifecycle methods on Topic and Subscription.
- Add publishMessages on PubSub for publishing multiple messages in a single RPC.
- Add RetrySettings and runWithRetry exponential backoff retry infrastructure.

feat(pubsub): add resilient parallel streaming pull

Add resilient multi-stream parallel Subscription.streamingPull
(maxConcurrentStreams) with automatic exponential backoff reconnection,
backpressure pause/resume forwarding, idle connection recovery,
streamingPullWithStream on PubSub, and routing of batched acknowledgments
and deadline modifications directly over active streaming channels.
refactor(pubsub): add streams to activeStreams only on listen and evict closed streams
style(pubsub): keep subscription name validation error message on single line
docs(pubsub): document error suppression rationale on responseStream.headers future
Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main' into pubsub-retry-batching

docs(pubsub): clarify batching semantics and add end-to-end batching tests

Addresses review feedback on #292:

- Document what `BatchingSettings.maxBytes` actually measures. Only the
  items themselves are counted, so unlike the Python client the per-request
  protobuf and gRPC overhead is excluded. Also document that an oversized
  item is sent alone in a batch that exceeds the limit, and note the
  server-side 10,000,000 byte limit that is not enforced here.
- Correct the default's unit comment: 1024 * 1024 is 1 MiB, not 1 MB.
- Explain the `+ 4` in the modify-ack-deadline item size: each ack ID is
  accompanied by its own int32 deadline in a parallel list.
- Add `batching_e2e_test.dart`, covering behaviour that the fake-based unit
  tests cannot: that a batched publish arrives as N distinct messages with N
  distinct server-assigned ids, that publishes spanning several batches all
  arrive, that `Topic.close()` flushes buffered messages, and that a batched
  acknowledgment actually reaches the server. Each test was verified to fail
  when the behaviour it covers is broken.
- Add a TODO referencing #346 for sharing retry logic with
  `google_cloud_storage`, and clarify that `totalTimeout` is the wall-clock
  budget across all attempts rather than a per-attempt cap.

fix(pubsub): do not drain a request stream that was already listened to

Tearing down a streaming pull connection called `stream.drain()` whenever
`StreamController.hasListener` was `false`. That predicate is `false` in two
very different situations: before the first listener subscribes, and after
that listener has canceled. In the second case `drain()` listens to an
already-consumed single-subscription stream and throws a `StateError`
synchronously, so the trailing `catchError` never ran, the error escaped
`cleanupCurrentConnection`, and reconnection stopped working entirely.

Introduce `DisposableStreamController`, which remembers whether its stream
was ever listened to and therefore only discards undelivered events when
doing so is safe. The drain itself is still required: the future returned by
`StreamController.close()` never completes while the stream has no listener.

This was caught by running the emulator-backed end-to-end suite, where
`streaming_pull_test.dart` failed with `Bad state: Stream has already been
listened to` followed by a 30 second timeout.

TAG=agy
CONV=4ecd3490-bbbe-499e-90e5-07ea5e14a460

fix(pubsub): measure batches the way the server measures requests

Batching counted only the items themselves — message payloads plus attribute
key and value bytes, or bare ack ID lengths. Pub/Sub validates the *serialized*
request (`PublishRequest.ByteSizeLong()`), which also includes the topic or
subscription field, the per-item tag and length prefix, and the attribute map
framing. `maxBytes` was therefore measuring something the server does not.

At the 1 MiB default the gap is 0.06% and harmless. It is not harmless once
`maxBytes` is raised: with it set to the documented 10,000,000 the real request
ran between 58 KB and 2 MB over the limit depending on message shape, and an
oversized request fails with a non-retryable INVALID_ARGUMENT that takes the
whole batch with it. Among the official clients we were the only one with
neither exact accounting nor a safety clamp: Python and Java count the framing
exactly, Go approximates and clamps, Node counts naively but clamps to 9 MiB.

More seriously, `AckSettings` shares `BatchingSettings` with publishing, so the
acknowledgment batchers inherited a 1 MiB ceiling against a 512 KB server limit
for `Acknowledge` and `ModifyAckDeadline` — twice what is allowed. Only
`maxMessages: 100` binding first kept this from firing, and because `_onAckBatch`
suppresses errors for fire-and-forget callers the symptom would not have been an
exception but indefinite redelivery of every message in the batch.

Sizes are computed arithmetically rather than by serializing: `itemSize` runs on
every add, and `package:protobuf` offers no cached size, only `writeToBuffer`.
Measured at 0.30 µs versus 0.29 µs for the old count, against 0.98 µs to
serialize.

Also caps settings to the applicable server limit rather than letting them
produce a request that cannot succeed, and corrects the modify-ack-deadline
comment: only `StreamingPullRequest` carries a deadline list parallel to its ack
IDs, so the estimate is conservative on the unary path.

fix(pubsub): address review of the batch size accounting

The CHANGELOG entry claimed resilient streaming pull and stream-routed
acknowledgment batches, neither of which exists on this branch — those bullets
belong to the stacked PR and were dragged in when the commit was moved between
branches. Removed, and the batching entry now states both caps and the fact
that the acknowledgment default dropped from 1 MiB.

`BatchingSettings` promised that a batch is "never knowingly sent over the
limit" a dozen lines before explaining that a single oversized item is sent
alone in a batch that exceeds it. The first is the paragraph a user consults to
decide whether they need to size-check their own messages, so it is now
explicit that they do.

`wire_size_test.dart` asserted against a local copy of the size function
labelled "Mirrors `Topic._publishedMessageSize`", so a change to the real one
would have left all 2,000 random cases green. Moved that function into
`wire_size.dart` as `publishRequestMessageSize` and pointed both the batcher
and the test at it.

The acknowledgment path had no byte-accounting tests at all, though it is the
path where a mistake is invisible: acknowledgments are fire-and-forget, so an
oversized request surfaces as redelivery rather than an exception. Added
`subscription_batching_test.dart`, which measures every recorded request with
`writeToBuffer()`. Its limits are deliberately tight — the fixed per-request
cost has to be a large enough share of `maxBytes` for its omission to change
the batch boundary — and reverting to the old accounting fails three of them.

Also closes a one-byte under-count: a unary `ModifyAckDeadlineRequest` carries
one shared `ackDeadlineSeconds`, whose tag the per-ack-ID estimate only covered
for groups of two or more. Its tag is now charged in the base size.

`varintSize` guarded its precondition with an assert alone, so a release build
would have returned 1 for a negative value that protobuf sign extends to ten
bytes. Currently unreachable — every caller validates first — but it now fails
in the over-estimating direction, which is the safe one for a size limit.

feat(pubsub)!: reject batch settings the server cannot accept

Asking for a `maxBytes` or `maxMessages` above the applicable Pub/Sub limit
used to be capped silently, matching Python, Go and Node. Throwing is better
here: `BatchingSettings` already throws for its other invalid inputs, so
clamping was the odd one out, and a capped value left the settings object
reporting a size that was not the one in use — `topic.publishSettings.batching
.maxBytes` would say 50,000,000 while batches flushed at 10,000,000.

The check cannot live in `BatchingSettings`, because which limit applies
depends on the request, and one instance may legitimately be shared between
`PublishSettings` and `AckSettings`. It is therefore made when the `Topic` or
`Subscription` is constructed, which is the first point at which the answer is
known, and still well before any RPC.

That leaves one case that must not throw. `maxBytes` defaults to 1 MiB, which
suits publishing and exceeds the 512,000 bytes an `Acknowledge` request
allows, so `AckSettings(batching: BatchingSettings(maxMessages: 50))` would
fail over a byte limit the caller never expressed an opinion about.
`BatchingSettings` now records whether `maxBytes` was supplied rather than
defaulted: a value the caller chose is validated, and the default is narrowed.
The field stays a non-nullable `int` with an unchanged default, so this is not
visible in the public API.

 ## 0.1.0-wip
 
-- Added resilient streaming pull in `Subscription.streamingPull` with support
-  for parallel streams (`maxConcurrentStreams`), automatic reconnection with
-  exponential backoff, and backpressure pause/resume forwarding.
-- Routed background `Subscription.acknowledge` and `modifyAckDeadline` batches
-  directly over active streaming pull channels.
-- Added `BatchingSettings`, `PublishSettings`, and `AckSettings`, and a
-  `publishSettings` parameter on `PubSub.topic`, `PubSub.topicName`,
-  `PubSub.createTopic` and the `Topic` constructors, and an `ackSettings`
-  parameter on `PubSub.subscription`, `PubSub.subscriptionName`,
-  `PubSub.createSubscription` and the `Subscription` constructors.
-  `BatchingSettings.maxBytes` is measured against the serialized request, the
-  same way Pub/Sub enforces its own limits, and defaults to 512,000 bytes, which
-  every request kind accepts. Creating a `Topic` or `Subscription` whose
-  settings exceed what the server accepts for the request being batched throws
-  an `ArgumentError`: 10,000,000 bytes and 1,000 messages for publishing,
-  512,000 bytes for acknowledgments and deadline modifications.
-- `Topic.publish` now buffers messages, sends them in batches, and retries
-  failed batches using `PublishSettings.retry`.
-- `Subscription.acknowledge` and `Subscription.modifyAckDeadline` now buffer
-  requests, send them in batches, and retry failed batches using
-  `AckSettings.retry`.

-- Re-exported `RetryRunner` and `ExponentialRetry` from
-  `package:google_cloud_rpc` and added `defaultRetry` to configure exponential
-  backoff retry parameters for Pub/Sub operations.
 - Initial release of the experimental Google Cloud Pub/Sub client.
-- Supports basic topic and subscription management.
-- Supports publishing and pulling messages (including streaming pull).
+- Topic and subscription creation and deletion (`PubSub`, `Topic`,
+  `Subscription`).
+- Message publishing with configurable background batching and exponential
+  backoff retries (`Topic.publish`, `PublishSettings`, `BatchingSettings`,
+  `defaultRetry`).
+- Synchronous (`Subscription.pull`) and resilient parallel streaming pull
+  (`Subscription.streamingPull`) with automatic reconnection and backpressure
+  handling.
+- Message acknowledgment and ack deadline modification with configurable
+  background batching (`Subscription.acknowledge`,
+  `Subscription.modifyAckDeadline`, `AckSettings`) and streaming pull channel
+  routing.

issue.title: feat(google_cloud_pubsub): add Subscription ack and modifyAckDeadline batching
issue.body_html:
Adds AckSettings and background batching and retry for
Subscription.acknowledge and Subscription.modifyAckDeadline.

  • Subscription.acknowledge(ReceivedMessage) and
    Subscription.modifyAckDeadline(ReceivedMessage, int) now buffer
    requests and flush them in batches according to
    AckSettings.batching, deduplicating ack IDs (and grouping by the
    latest deadline per ack ID) and retrying transient failures using
    AckSettings.retry.
  • Subscription validates ackSettings.batching on construction
    against the 512,000-byte server limit for Acknowledge and
    ModifyAckDeadline requests.
  • Added Subscription.close() and Subscription.isClosed to flush
    buffered acknowledgments and deadline modifications and await
    in-flight batches before shutdown.
  • Subscription.modifyAckDeadline, Subscription.modifyAckDeadlineNow,
    PubSub.modifyAckDeadline, and ReceivedMessage.modifyAckDeadline
    validate that ackDeadlineSeconds is between 0 and 600 seconds;
    PubSub.pull validates maxMessages > 0 and PubSub.streamingPull
    validates streamAckDeadlineSeconds synchronously.
  • Message now always copies data (Uint8List.fromList) and wraps
    attributes in Map.unmodifiable.
  • Added ReceivedMessage.deliveryAttempt and toString() on Message
    and ReceivedMessage, and made ReceivedMessage.acknowledge and
    ReceivedMessage.modifyAckDeadline throw StateError when no
    handler is configured.

Part 4 of 5 (followed by #339).

issue.title: Share retry logic between google_cloud_pubsub and google_cloud_storage (before pubsub 1.0)
issue.body_html:
google_cloud_pubsub and google_cloud_storage each have their own retry
implementation, and the ServiceException half of the retryability predicate
(408/429/500/502/503/504) is currently duplicated verbatim between them.

  • pkgs/google_cloud_pubsub/lib/src/retry.dart — RetrySettings data class
    (validated, non-const, ==/hashCode), plus @internal delaySequence,
    isRetryable, runWithRetry. Only RetrySettings is exported.
  • pkgs/google_cloud_storage/lib/src/retry.dart — sealed RetryRunner /
    ExponentialRetry / NoDelayRetry / const defaultRetry, exported
    wholesale and threaded through ~39 public signatures.

Context: #292

Suggested order

  1. Share the internals first (delaySequence, runWithRetry, and the
    ServiceException arm of the predicate). This is invisible to users and
    needs no public API decision.
  2. Only then consider unifying the public settings type.

Open questions to resolve first

  • Home package. package:google_cloud_rpc is the only package both
    already depend on (^0.6.0), but it is generated: lib/rpc.dart is not in
    librarian's keep list, so hand-written lib/retry.dart +
    lib/src/retry.dart + tests must each be added to keep, and clock added
    to its dependencies — which makes clock transitive for every generated
    REST package. It must also stay free of package:grpc.
  • const vs validation. defaultRetry is a const default parameter
    value in ~39 storage signatures, so a merged type must have a const
    constructor — which cannot have a body. But asserts cannot express the
    Duration invariants at all (assert(initialDelay > Duration.zero) in a
    const constructor is a compile error: "In constant expressions, operands of
    this operator must be of type 'num'"    ), and the int/double asserts that
    can be written do not run under dart run or dart compile exe. So
    unifying the type means losing eager ArgumentError validation unless a
    separate checkValid() is introduced and called from every non-const
    boundary.
  • NoDelayRetry. It is const ... (initialDelay: Duration.zero, maxDelay: Duration.zero), which pubsub's validation explicitly rejects.
  • Jitter. pubsub applies ±20%; storage applies none. Unifying changes
    storage's runtime retry timing.
  • Defaults must stay per-service. pubsub 100 ms / ×1.3 / 1 min vs storage
    1 s / ×2 / 2 min. Do not share defaultRetry.
  • Naming. pubsub's totalTimeout matches GAX; storage's
    maxRetryInterval reads like a per-attempt cap, which is actually
    maxDelay.

Constraint

Move the declaration and re-export it — never introduce a second same-named
type. Two RetrySettings declarations would be an ambiguous import for anyone
using both packages.

Until this is done, any fix to retryability must be applied to both copies.

issue.title: test(pubsub): run the Pub/Sub end-to-end tests against Google Cloud
issue.body_html:
The eight Pub/Sub end-to-end tests were only ever run against the
emulator. They were already written to work against either backend
(test/test_utils.dart picks up application default credentials when
PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST is unset, and a couple of them already branch on
isEmulator), but nothing selected them in the Cloud Build integration
job, and the project did not have the API enabled in Terraform.

Terraform

  • Enable pubsub.googleapis.com in .gcb/builds/services/main.tf.

Tests

  • Tag the eight end-to-end tests google-cloud in addition to
    firebase-emulator. .gcb/scripts/integration.sh runs
    dart test . -P google-cloud from the repo root, so the root
    dart_test.yaml governs, and it already defines the tag and the
    preset. Nothing in .gcb/ needs to change.

    I verified that a file tagged with both firebase-emulator and
    google-cloud really is selected by -P google-cloud from the repo
    root and by -P firebase-emulator from inside the package, and is
    still excluded from a plain dart test.

  • Declare the google-cloud tag and preset in the package's own
    dart_test.yaml and exclude it by default. Without this, a plain
    dart test from inside pkgs/google_cloud_pubsub would run the tests
    against whatever project the developer's credentials point at.

  • Replace the DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch name suffixes with
    a random suffix (testResourceName), following the pattern in
    google_cloud_storage's test_utils.dart. Against the shared
    dart-sdk-testing project two builds can now overlap, and a shared
    name would make one of them fail with a ConflictException or observe
    the other's messages.

Verification

dart format, dart analyze clean; dart test . and
dart test -P firebase-emulator (14 tests) pass locally.

issue.title: feat(google_cloud_pubsub): add Batcher and Topic publish batching
issue.body_html:
Adds background batching and retry to Topic.publish, configured with
the new PublishSettings and BatchingSettings.

Batching lets many Topic.publish calls share one Publish RPC instead
of making one RPC per message. Other Pub/Sub clients (Python, Go, Node,
Java) batch in the same way.

Behavior changes

  • Topic.publish no longer sends right away. It buffers the message
    and returns a future that completes once the batch is sent. A batch
    is sent when it reaches maxMessages (default 100) or maxBytes
    (default 512,000 bytes), or after maxDelay (default 10 ms).
  • Call and await Topic.close() to flush buffered messages before
    shutdown. PubSub.close() does not flush topics. After
    PubSub.close(), publishing fails immediately with a StateError
    rather than retrying the closed channel's UNAVAILABLE errors.
  • Only messages published through the same Topic object share
    batches, so a Topic should be created once and reused.
  • Topic.publish copies data and attributes, so changing them after
    the call does not change the published message.
  • Topic.create() now returns the same Topic (keeping its settings)
    instead of a new one.
  • PubSub.publish is still one unbatched RPC with no retry. It now
    throws InternalServerErrorException if the response has no message
    ID. The new PubSub.publishMessages that Topic uses is
    @internal.

Details

  • BatchingSettings.maxBytes is compared with the size of the
    serialized PublishRequest, the same size the server checks. This
    includes the topic name and the protobuf framing of each message and
    attribute. lib/src/wire_size.dart works out the size arithmetically,
    because package:protobuf has no way to get a message's size without
    serializing it. A test checks the result against writeToBuffer().
  • Settings above the server limits (10,000,000 bytes or 1,000 messages
    per Publish request) throw an ArgumentError when the Topic is
    created. PubSub.createTopic checks this before the CreateTopic
    RPC, so invalid settings don't leave a new topic behind.
  • maxBytes defaults to 512,000 bytes rather than the ~1 MB other
    clients use for publishing. BatchingSettings is also used for
    acknowledgments in #292, whose server limit is 512,000 bytes, so one
    default that fits every request kind avoids special-casing.
  • A failed batch is retried with PublishSettings.retry (default
    defaultRetry from #353). Publish is retried even though a retry
    can produce a duplicate message. This is consistent with Pub/Sub's
    at-least-once delivery. If the batch still fails, every future in
    the batch completes with the error. If the server returns fewer
    message IDs than messages, the messages without an ID fail.

Not included yet

  • Publisher flow control (limits on buffered and in-flight messages).
    There is a TODO on Topic.publish, and it is planned as a follow-up.
  • A per-attempt deadline on Publish requests (TODO on
    Topic.publish). Until then, a hung request keeps its futures and
    Topic.close() pending.
  • Ordering keys.

Split out from #292 (3/4).

pull.body:
Adds background batching and retry to `Topic.publish`, configured with
the new `PublishSettings` and `BatchingSettings`.

Batching lets many `Topic.publish` calls share one `Publish` RPC instead
of making one RPC per message. Other Pub/Sub clients (Python, Go, Node,
Java) batch in the same way.

**Behavior changes**

- `Topic.publish` no longer sends right away. It buffers the message
  and returns a future that completes once the batch is sent. A batch
  is sent when it reaches `maxMessages` (default 100) or `maxBytes`
  (default 512,000 bytes), or after `maxDelay` (default 10 ms).
- Call and await `Topic.close()` to flush buffered messages before
  shutdown. `PubSub.close()` does not flush topics. After
  `PubSub.close()`, publishing fails immediately with a `StateError`
  rather than retrying the closed channel's UNAVAILABLE errors.
- Only messages published through the same `Topic` object share
  batches, so a `Topic` should be created once and reused.
- `Topic.publish` copies `data` and `attributes`, so changing them after
  the call does not change the published message.
- `Topic.create()` now returns the same `Topic` (keeping its settings)
  instead of a new one.
- `PubSub.publish` is still one unbatched RPC with no retry. It now
  throws `InternalServerErrorException` if the response has no message
  ID. The new `PubSub.publishMessages` that `Topic` uses is
  `@internal`.

issue.title: feat(pubsub): add resilient parallel streaming pull
issue.body_html:
Adds resilient parallel streaming pull to Subscription.streamingPull
and routes batched acknowledgments and deadline modifications over
active streams when available.

  • Subscription.streamingPull opens maxConcurrentStreams parallel
    StreamingPull connections and multiplexes their messages onto a
    single returned Stream<ReceivedMessage>.
  • Reconnects automatically with exponential backoff (RetryRunner) when
    a stream fails with a retryable error or closes unexpectedly, and
    resets the retry state once a stream receives a message or remains
    connected for at least 15 seconds.
  • When maxConcurrentStreams > 1, an individual stream exhausting its
    retries does not terminate the combined stream while sibling streams
    remain active.
  • Batched acknowledgments and deadline modifications from
    Subscription.acknowledge, Subscription.modifyAckDeadline,
    ReceivedMessage.acknowledge, and
    ReceivedMessage.modifyAckDeadline are written to an active
    StreamingPull request stream when one is open, falling back to
    unary RPCs with retry when no stream is active.
  • Propagates pause and resume across all active underlying streams,
    and in Subscription.close() cancels active streaming pulls before
    flushing pending batches via unary RPCs.
  • Adds PubSub.streamingPullWithStream for bidirectional
    request/response stream management.

Stacked on #292.
